Heatwave fire spree 'busiest in boss's 26-year career'
Paul BurnellNorth West
Fire chiefs in Greater Manchester have said the service is experiencing its busiest period in decades - as a series of serious blazes broke out at the peak of the recent UK heatwave.
A raft of fires across the country, including devastating blazes in the West Midlands, later prompted the government to issue a temporary ban on disposable barbecues.
Greater Manchester's Chief Fire Officer Dave Russel thanked crews for their work in an "exceptionally busy period" while his deputy Jim Willmott said firefighters had received 1,200 calls on Thursday.
Willmott told BBC Radio Manchester: "Yesterday I was in the fire control room for North West Fire Control - it really was the most incredibly busy period I have ever seen in my 26 years of service."
Earlier in the month crews stood down from wildfires on two stretches of moorland near Dove Stone Reservoir and at Tintwistle and Swineshore.
The fire chief said a lot of the recent incidents were "very reminiscent of the prolonged wildfires of 2018 and some we saw in 2022".
On Thursday the control room dealt with 1,200 calls logged as 360 incidents, from wildfires to road accidents, he said.
He said the Saddleworth Moor fire near Holmfirth Road was now well under control but firefighters would stay there over the weekend.
He said the kits are "a recipe for wildfires" as they are designed to stay very hot, even with liquid inside.
Willmott added: "Over the years I have been to so many moorland fires and wildfires caused by disposable barbecues. Anything that reduces that has to be good."

Walking through forest cools body faster than city streets during heat wave: study
Listen
By Jhoo Dong-chan
Published KST
Thermal images comparing heat strains on the human body while walking through a forest and city street / Courtesy of Korea Forest Service
Walking through a forest trail lowers the heat strain on the human body significantly faster than walking on asphalt roads in the city, according to a field experiment by the National Institute of Forest Science, a research body under the Korea Forest Service, conducted amid Korea's ongoing summer heat wave.
The institute tested the cooling effect of Hongneung Forest, an experimental forest in Dongdaemun District that dates to the Joseon era, by using thermal imaging cameras to compare pedestrians' heat response while walking on a forest trail versus a nearby asphalt road.
Participants who walked the forest trail saw their average facial surface temperature drop by as much as 1.9 degrees Celsius from their starting point, and it stayed about 1.7 degrees lower even after the walk ended. On the asphalt road, by contrast, the average facial surface temperature — 37.0 degrees Celsius at the start — jumped to 38.1 degrees in the first stretch and showed little improvement by the end. Averaged over the full route, facial surface temperatures were 1.1 degrees lower on the forest trail than on the asphalt road.
The institute attributed the cooling effect to dense tree canopies blocking direct solar radiation and to transpiration from leaves, which lowers the surrounding temperature and eases the heat load on pedestrians.
Large green spaces such as Hongneung Forest play an important role in easing heat waves and the urban heat island effect, the institute said, noting the forest's significance is especially pronounced in Dongdaemun District, which has limited green space.
According to the Korea Forest Service's urban forest spatial database, Hongneung Forest spans 35.4 hectares, or about 14 percent of the district's total forested area of 251.6 hectares, making it the largest single forest tract in the district.
An institute researcher at the Urban Forests for Living Environment Research Center said the study confirmed that forests not only lower surrounding air temperature but also meaningfully reduce the heat strain felt by people who use them, adding that preserving the function and value of large urban forests like Hongneung Forest is essential for responding to heat waves and the urban heat island effect.

articles.title: Assam floods: Bihubor survivors face fresh hardship as receding waters leave homes buried in mud, silt - India Today NE
articles.full_text:
Assam floods: Bihubor survivors face fresh hardship as receding waters leave homes buried in mud, silt
In Bihubor, receding floodwaters have left homes, roads and courtyards buried under mud and silt. Families now face damaged houses, lost belongings and prolonged disruption to work, travel and schooling.
Life remains far from normal in Bihubor, one of the worst-affected areas of Assam’s devastating floods, as receding waters leave behind thick layers of mud and silt across homes, roads and courtyards.
While floodwaters have withdrawn from some areas, the accumulation of silt has created a fresh challenge for residents trying to return home and rebuild their lives. Several houses remain severely damaged, forcing families to live in cramped conditions or makeshift shelters along roadsides.
In some households, as many as 10 to 12 family members are being forced to stay in a single room. Residents said they are struggling to clean their homes while coping with the loss of household belongings, livestock, important documents and livelihoods.
Local resident Indu Devi said her family had lost almost everything after the floodwaters entered their home suddenly. Although food and other essential supplies are currently available, she said most household belongings were destroyed and around 10 family members are now staying together in one room.
In several parts of Bihubor, the situation remains critical as floodwaters have not completely receded even after weeks. Some residents said they have not been able to return to their homes for nearly 20 to 25 days.
Binita Gogol, another resident, said floodwaters that entered her home on July 20 have still not completely receded. She said livestock, household belongings and documents related to her children's education were destroyed.
Transportation has also emerged as a major challenge, with residents in some affected areas still required to travel one to two kilometres by boat to reach their homes or access essential services.
Another resident, Joon Dekha, said her family managed to escape the sudden rise in floodwaters but lost most of their belongings. With her daughter studying in Class 10 and son in Class 5, she said she is now worried about continuing their education while her husband works as a daily-wage labourer.
The devastation has left many families facing an uncertain future, even as the immediate threat from rising water begins to ease.
Assam has recorded more than 100 flood-related deaths, while thousands of people have been displaced across several districts amid the ongoing flood situation.
